questions.q: A torque is the turning effect of a force acting on an object. What is the SI unit of torque?
options: the joule (J)
the newton metre (N m)
the newton (N)
the newton per metre (N m⁻¹)
questions.explanation: Torque is the turning effect of a force, and its SI unit is the newton metre (N m). Even though a newton metre is dimensionally the same as a joule, torque is not energy, so writing joules here is a marked error.

questions.q: As a current-carrying coil rotates in a motor, what happens to the magnitude of the forces acting on the sides LK and MN, and to the torque acting on the coil?
options: Both the forces and the torque stay constant throughout the rotation
The magnitude of the forces remains constant, but the torque acting on the coil changes in magnitude
The forces decrease as the coil rotates, so the torque decreases with them
The forces change but the torque stays constant
questions.explanation: The magnitude of the forces acting on sides LK and MN remains constant throughout the rotation, because those sides stay perpendicular to the field. However, the torque acting on the coil changes in magnitude as the perpendicular distance to the pivot line changes.

questions.q: The force on the sides of a coil that are perpendicular to the magnetic field is F = BIl sin θ. If the coil has n turns of wire, what is the force on these sides?
options: F = BIl sin θ, unchanged by the number of turns
F = nBIl sin θ, n times greater because of the n turns
F = BIl sin θ / n
F = nBIl, with no dependence on the angle
questions.explanation: Real motor rotors have many turns of wire. If the coil has n turns, these sides experience a force n times greater, F = nBIl sin θ, and this extra force increases the torque acting on the sides of the coil.

questions.q: A coil contains 15 loops and its plane is sitting at an angle of 30° to the direction of a magnetic field of 7.6 mT. The coil has an area of 9.6 × 10⁻³ m² and a 15 mA current passes through it. Determine the magnitude of the torque acting on the coil.
questions.explanation: Direct substitution into τ = nBIA cos θ, where θ is the angle between the plane of the coil and the magnetic field. The answer 1.4 × 10⁻⁵ N m matches the textbook worked example.

questions.q: A lever is free to rotate about a point P. A force of 24 N acts at right angles to the lever at a distance of 0.75 m from P. Calculate the magnitude of the torque acting on the lever.
working: Because the force is perpendicular to the line joining P to the point of application, \(\tau = Fd\)
questions.explanation: When the force is perpendicular to the line joining the pivot point and the point of application, torque is simply τ = Fd = 24 × 0.75 = 18 N m. The SI unit is the newton metre.

questions.q: In the formula τ = nBIA cos θ for the torque on a coil, what does the angle θ represent?
options: The angle between the normal to the coil and the magnetic field
The angle between the plane of the coil and the magnetic field
The angle between the current and the area vector
The angle through which the coil has spun from rest
questions.explanation: In the textbook convention τ = nBIA cos θ, where θ is the angle between the plane of the coil and the magnetic field. So θ = 0 (plane parallel to the field) gives cos 0 = 1 and maximum torque; θ = 90° gives zero torque.

questions.q: The commutator is a mechanical switch consisting of a split metal ring. What does it do as the coil of a DC motor rotates?
options: It increases the magnetic field strength when the torque falls to zero
It automatically changes the direction of the current flowing through the coil when the torque falls to zero, so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction
It keeps the current direction fixed so the coil rocks back and forth
It connects the coil to slip rings to deliver alternating current
questions.explanation: The commutator is a mechanical switch made of a split metal ring connected to each end of the coil. It automatically changes the direction of the current through the coil when the torque falls to zero, so the momentum carries the coil past and it keeps rotating in the same direction instead of rocking back and forth.

questions.q: From memory: as a current-carrying coil rotates, the magnitude of the forces on its active sides stays constant, yet the torque acting on the coil changes. Explain why the torque changes.
keyPoints: The two active sides stay perpendicular to the field, so each force stays constant at B I L the whole way round.
What changes is the perpendicular distance (lever arm) between the axis of rotation and the lines of action of the forces.

Torque = force × perpendicular distance, so when the lever arm is largest (plane parallel to field) the torque is maximum, and when the forces act along the axis (plane perpendicular to field) the lever arm is zero and the torque is zero.
questions.explanation: If you said the force stays constant and the lever arm (perpendicular distance) is what changes, grade Good or Easy. If you said the force decreases as the coil rotates, that is the marked error — grade Again or Hard.

questions.q: From memory: why do the two equal and opposite motor-effect forces on the active sides of the loop make it spin on its axle rather than fly sideways across the field?
keyPoints: The current runs in opposite directions on the two active sides, so the forces are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.
The two forces are offset from the central axis, so they form a couple (a pair of moments).
A couple produces a net turning effect (torque) but zero net translational force, so the coil rotates without being pushed across the field.
questions.explanation: The key word the marker wants is couple: equal, opposite, offset forces giving rotation without translation. If you described the coil 'being pushed across the field', that is wrong — grade Again.

questions.q: You may see torque written as nBIA cos θ or as nBIA sin θ. Why are both correct, and how do you choose?
options: They describe different physics, so you should always use whichever your formula sheet shows

They are the same physics with θ defined differently — cos θ when θ is measured to the plane of the coil, sin θ when θ is measured to the normal — so you read which angle the question gives and pick the matching function
Cosine is for single loops and sine is for multi-turn coils
Sine is only correct when the current is alternating
questions.explanation: The two angles are complements (they add to 90°) and cos of one equals sin of the other, so both describe the identical curve. Use cos θ when θ is the angle to the plane of the coil, and sin θ (the NESA sheet's convention) when θ is the angle to the normal. The number-one mark-loser is misreading which angle θ refers to.
